questions.title: Is the entropy definition for patching missing a minus sign?
questions.question_body:
In Section 2.3 (Entropy Patching), the entropy used to select patch boundaries is defined as

$H(x_i) = \sum_{v \in \mathcal{V}} p_e(x_i=v\mid \mathbf{x}_{<i}) \log p_e(x_i=v\mid \mathbf{x}_{<i})$.

Standard Shannon entropy is $-\sum p \log p$. If we omit the minus sign, $H(x_i)$ would be non-positive and higher uncertainty would correspond to more negative values. Is the minus sign intentionally omitted here (e.g., with thresholds adapted accordingly), or is this a typographical error? How are thresholds $\theta_g$ and $\theta_r$ interpreted if $H$ is negative?

questions.title: What is the exact algorithm for the approximate monotonicity entropy patching rule?
questions.question_body:
Section 2.3 introduces a relative criterion $H(x_t) - H(x_{t-1}) > \theta_r$ described as breaking approximate monotonically decreasing entropy within a patch. Could you spell out the full boundary selection procedure?

- How is the first patch initialized and when do you close it?
- Do you enforce any smoothing (e.g., moving averages) or hysteresis to avoid rapid toggling near the threshold?
- Are there minimum/maximum patch length constraints with this rule?
- How do you combine the global threshold and the relative threshold if both are used?
- Pseudocode for the segmentation pass would be very helpful.

questions.title: During generation, who decides patch boundaries and how is that decision computed online?
questions.question_body:
The paper says BLT must decide at each byte whether it is at a patch boundary, since that determines whether to invoke the (expensive) latent transformer step. In training, boundaries are precomputed from an entropy model. At inference time:

- Is the same entropy model run online to compute $H(x_i)$ on the partial generation history and then thresholded?
- If yes, does this overhead enter the inference FLOPs accounting? If no, how are boundaries chosen without future context?
- How sensitive is decoding quality and latency to the inference-time threshold choice (e.g., your 0.6 to 0.1 adjustment)?

questions.title: In the FLOPs equations, what exactly does $n_p$ denote and what are $k$ and $r$?
questions.question_body:
In Section 4.6 (FLOPs Estimation), $n_p$ appears to sometimes refer to the number of patches and elsewhere to patch size. For example, $P \in \mathbb{R}^{n_p \times h_{\mathcal{G}}}$ suggests $n_p$ is the number of patches, while $m=n_{ctx}/n_p$ suggests $n_p$ is the average patch size. Could you disambiguate the symbols and restate the FLOPs terms with:

- $L_b$: number of bytes in the sequence,
- $L_p$: number of patches in the sequence,
- $s = L_b/L_p$: average patch size in bytes,
- any other quantities (e.g., $k$, $r$) with clear definitions and shapes for $Q,K,V$?

A worked example with actual dimensions for one model scale would help.

questions.title: Why can the local encoder attend across patch boundaries if cross-attention queries only attend within their patch?
questions.question_body: Section 3.2 says the local encoder uses local block-causal attention that can cross dynamic patch boundaries, but the encoder cross-attention mask restricts each query to attend only to bytes in its own patch. Does this create a situation where patch $j$'s pooled bytes already carry context from earlier patches via the encoder self-attention, effectively leaking cross-patch information? If so, is this intentional to make patch representations context-aware? How do you prevent lookahead leakage across patches (i.e., future bytes) given the causal mask?

questions.title: In the decoder cross-attention, do bytes attend only to their own patch representation, and how is causality preserved?
questions.question_body: Section 3.3 reverses the roles of queries and keys/values in decoder cross-attention. Is there a patch-specific mask so that bytes in patch $j$ only attend to $o_j$ (and not to $o_{j+1}$)? Also, within a patch, is there any masking to keep the byte-level process causal (e.g., byte $i$ in patch $j$ not attending to decoder states corresponding to future bytes in the same patch), or is causality fully handled by the subsequent decoder transformer layer?

questions.title: How are the patch queries initialized in encoder cross-attention?
questions.question_body:
The text mentions initializing $P_{0,j}$ by pooling the byte representations of patch $p_j$ and later specifies max-pooling for the first encoder cross-attention layer. Could you clarify:

- Is pooling max, mean, or something learned (e.g., attention pooling)?
- At deeper encoder layers, is pooling recomputed on the updated $h_{l-1,i}$, or are queries persistent across layers?
- Do you use any learned per-patch positional features during pooling (e.g., start-of-patch indicator)?

questions.title: Without positional encodings in cross-attention, how is intra-patch order modeled?
questions.question_body: The cross-attention modules omit positional embeddings, yet order within a patch seems important. My understanding is that the byte representations $h_{l-1,i}$ from the local encoder already encode order via RoPE used in self-attention. Is that the only source of order in cross-attention? Could cross-attention benefit from explicit relative positions between the query (patch) and key/value (bytes) to improve alignment, or did you find it unnecessary/harmful?

questions.title: What is the exact forward/generation pipeline in BLT at inference time?
questions.question_body:
I want to understand the step-by-step generation loop:

- As bytes are generated, does the local encoder re-encode the most recent window of bytes to produce/refresh the current patch representation input $p_j$ to the global model?
- When a patch boundary is detected, is the global transformer stepped once to produce a new $o_j$, which the local decoder then uses to autoregressively produce the bytes for that patch?
- What is cached across time (e.g., global transformer KV, local encoder states) to make this efficient given variable patch boundaries?

questions.title: How do you calibrate the entropy threshold to hit a target average patch size?
questions.question_body:
Section 4.3 says the entropy threshold is chosen to achieve a desired average patch size on the pretraining mix. Practically:

- Do you sweep $\theta$ over a sample of the pretraining data and pick the value that yields the target average size $s$?
- How sensitive is the achieved $s$ to domain shifts between training and evaluation (e.g., code vs. prose)?
- At inference time you adjust the threshold (0.6 to 0.1) to improve accuracy. Do you remeasure and accept the higher compute, or do you also cap patch counts?

questions.title: Are there explicit min/max patch length constraints to avoid degenerate segments?
questions.question_body: Dynamic patching can, in principle, produce extremely long patches in very predictable regions and very short patches in noisy bursts. Do you enforce any hard constraints like a minimum or maximum patch length in bytes? If not, do you observe heavy tails in the patch length distribution, and how do you mitigate memory spikes (beyond the training-time padding/truncation to 12k/24k bytes mentioned)?

questions.title: Does the FLOPs accounting include the cost of the entropy model at inference?
questions.question_body: In the FLOPs section, the total per-byte FLOPs sum encoder, global, decoder, and cross-attentions, but I do not see the cost of running the entropy model online to set boundaries. At training time you precompute boundaries during dataloading, but at inference time you adjust thresholds and seemingly must run the entropy model. Is this overhead included in the reported inference FLOPs, and if not, how large is it relative to the latent transformer step?

questions.title: How are batches packed to both equalize bytes and keep a fixed number of patches per batch?
questions.question_body:
Section 4.3 says you keep the number of bytes per batch constant in expectation to avoid giving larger patch sizes an unfair context advantage. But it also says you pack batches of patches so every batch has the same number of patches, and you pad/truncate byte sequences to fixed limits to avoid memory spikes. Could you detail the batching algorithm that reconciles:

- constant expected bytes per batch,
- constant number of patches per batch (to avoid padding in the latent transformer),
- per-sequence byte caps (12k/24k),
- and fairness across patch-size settings?

questions.title: Why do larger patch sizes scale better at larger model/data scales?
questions.question_body:
In Section 5.1 and 5.3 you observe that BLT with average patch size around 8 bytes starts worse at small scale but overtakes BPE and smaller-patch BLT at larger model/data scales. Can you elaborate on the mechanism? Is it because:

- the local encoder/decoder FLOPs become a smaller fraction as the global model grows,
- the global model benefits from fewer, more informative steps,
- or reduced LM head cost (since output vocab is 256) allows reallocating compute more effectively?

Any empirical breakdown of FLOPs vs. error across modules would help.

questions.title: Is BPB directly comparable across BLT and BPE models, and how does it relate to perplexity?
questions.question_body: You report Bits-Per-Byte (BPB) as a tokenizer-independent measure: $\mathrm{BPB}(x) = \mathcal{L}_{CE}(\mathbf{x}) / (\ln 2 \cdot n_{\text{bytes}})$. If I want to compare to token-level perplexity for a BPE model with average bytes per token $\bar{b}$, is the relationship approximately $\mathrm{BPB} \approx (\ln \mathrm{ppl}_\text{token}) / (\ln 2 \cdot \bar{b})$? Are there pitfalls when the byte distribution differs substantially across corpora (e.g., more UTF-8 multi-byte characters)?

questions.title: How do hash $n$-gram embeddings handle collisions, and why normalize by the number of $n$-grams plus one?
questions.question_body:
Section 3.2.1 adds hash embeddings for $n$-grams ($n=3\dots 8$) with separate tables $E_n^{hash}$ and aggregates them as $e_i = x_i + \sum_n E_n^{hash}(\mathrm{Hash}(g_{i,n}))$, then normalizes by the number of sizes plus one. Questions:

- How significant are collisions at your chosen table sizes (e.g., 500k), and do you apply any multi-hash or de-collision techniques?
- Why normalize by the count (vs. scale by $1/\sqrt{\text{count}}$)?
- Do you include language/script ID or any other features to reduce cross-language collisions in $n$-grams?

questions.title: How does Space Patching handle non-Latin scripts and mixed-language text?
questions.question_body: Space Patching defines 'space-like' bytes as anything not a Latin letter, digit, or UTF-8 continuation byte, and requires each patch to contain at least one non-space-like byte. In multilingual datasets with scripts that do not use spaces or have different word boundary conventions, does this heuristic create too many or too few boundaries? Do you have empirical patch length distributions by script, and do you observe any degradation vs. entropy-based patching in such languages?

questions.title: Where exactly is the byte-level language modeling loss applied in BLT?
questions.question_body: Since the latent transformer operates on patch representations and the local decoder maps patch representations to byte distributions with a 256-sized output projection, am I correct that the next-byte cross-entropy loss is applied only at the local decoder's output? Does the global transformer ever directly predict bytes (e.g., via auxiliary losses), or is it only trained through gradients flowing back from the decoder?

questions.title: How is block-causal attention defined across multiple documents when you pack sequences?
questions.question_body:
You mention packing examples to avoid padding in the latent transformer and using a block-causal mask that 'restricts attention to be up to and including the current patch within the current document'. When multiple documents are concatenated in a batch:

- Are patch indices and positional encodings reset at document boundaries?
- How is the attention mask constructed to prevent any cross-document attention at both byte and patch levels?
- Does packing impact KV-cache reuse at inference time?

questions.title: What causes 'entropy drift' and why does resetting the entropy model context at newlines help?
questions.question_body:
Section 4.4 mentions that structured, repetitive content (e.g., MMLU formats) leads to progressively larger patches due to lower entropy in the entropy model's context ('entropy drift'). Could you explain:

- What precisely causes entropy to drop over long repetitive templates?
- How does resetting the entropy model’s context at newlines counteract this effect?
- Why does the approximate monotonicity rule suffer less from drift than the global threshold?

questions.title: Why use RoPE in self-attention but no positional encoding in cross-attention?
questions.question_body: All self-attention layers use RoPE with $\theta=500000$, but the cross-attention modules have no positional encodings. Did you test adding relative positions in cross-attention (e.g., between patch queries and byte keys)? If tried and removed, what degradation did you observe? If not tried, what’s the intuition for excluding positional signals in cross-attention while including them in self-attention?

questions.title: When initializing from Llama 3.1, was the global transformer frozen or fine-tuned?
questions.question_body: Section 6.2 says you initialize the global transformer from Llama 3.1 and then 'update the weights ... using one-tenth the learning rate,' but later the text also describes 'initializing and freezing the global transformer.' Which protocol did you use for the reported results: fully frozen global transformer, low-LR fine-tuning, or a mix across phases? Any insights on stability and sample efficiency across these choices?

questions.title: Can entropy-based patching split UTF-8 multibyte code points, and does that matter?
questions.question_body: Since BLT models raw bytes, entropy-based patching could place boundaries inside a UTF-8 multibyte character. Do you explicitly prevent splits within a multibyte code point? If not, does this negatively impact multilingual performance or robustness, and did you measure any difference when enforcing code point alignment of boundaries?

questions.title: How is KV caching implemented when patch boundaries are adaptive during generation?
questions.question_body:
Adaptive patching means the number and positions of latent transformer steps depend on the evolving entropy and thresholds. For efficient decoding:

- Do you maintain a KV cache at the patch level for the global transformer that is updated only at boundaries?
- How do you handle partial patches when a boundary is shifted by a threshold change mid-generation?
- Are there any trade-offs in cache invalidation compared to a fixed-tokenization LM with regular step cadence?
